text:
American cities have undergone dramatic economic and demographic transformation since 1980, with gentrification accelerating significantly after 2000 [Source: ev-1]. The rate of gentrification doubled in the period following 2000 compared to the 1990s, affecting nearly 20% of lower-income neighborhoods in major cities [Source: ev-1]. Portland experienced the most intensive gentrification with 58.1% of eligible tracts transforming, followed by Washington D.C. at 51.9%, Minneapolis at 50.6%, and Seattle at 50% [Source: ev-1]. This transformation was driven partly by a shift from income-based patterns that were rare between 1970 and 1980 to dominant forms by 2000 through 2020 [Source: ev-1].

Inequality has risen sharply across metropolitan areas, creating stark divides between high and low-income residents despite general nominal wealth growth [Source: ev-1]. The U.S. Gini coefficient reached 0.40 in 2013, while New York City led major metros with a coefficient of 0.5469 [Source: ev-1]. Atlanta and Miami recorded coefficients of 0.57, and New Orleans reached 0.56 [Source: ev-1]. Several metros exhibit extreme inequality patterns with Gini coefficients exceeding 0.54 and income ratios reaching 18:1 between top and bottom earners [Source: ev-1]. Specifically, the 95/20 income ratio shows Atlanta and Washington D.C. at 18:1, meaning the 95th percentile earns 18 times more than the 20th percentile [Source: ev-1].

Affordability has deteriorated significantly as costs outpaced income growth since 2000. Home prices increased by 177% while median household income grew only 92% during this period [Source: ev-1]. The Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024, representing a 225% increase since January 2000 [Source: ev-1]. Price-to-income ratios in California cities range between 9.6 and 12.2, which is more than double the national average of 4.7 [Source: ev-1].

Displacement and worsening economic mobility are evident across most major metros. Forty-eight of the largest 50 metropolitan areas experienced worsening economic mobility for low-income families over a 15-year period [Source: ev-1]. Only Houston showed an improvement in income outcomes for people growing up in the 1990 compared to those from the 1980s, with a gain of just 1.1% [Source: ev-1]. In gentrifying neighborhoods, poverty rates decreased by 0.7 percentage points as populations became whiter and increased, whereas non-gentrifying low-income areas saw poverty increase by 6.7 percentage points alongside slight population losses [Source: ev-1]. Residents from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tend to move to poorer non-gentrifying areas, while residents from other such neighborhoods move to wealthier locations [Source: ev-1].

Demographic shifts further characterize this four-decade transformation. Since 2000, the white population share fell by 7 points in urban cores and 8 points in suburbs [Source: ev-1]. Currently, 53% of urban counties are majority nonwhite compared to only 10% of suburban counties [Source: ev-1]. Nearly 80% of the country's under-45 population growth since 1980 was concentrated in metro areas with over 1 million residents [Source: ev-1]. Urban counties gained prime-age workers aged 25 to 54 while rural counties lost this demographic group [Source: ev-1]. Educational attainment has also shifted, with urban areas now having 35% of residents holding bachelor's degrees or higher, compared to 31% in suburbs and 19% in rural areas [Source: ev-1].

The labor market transformation contributed to these changes as manufacturing jobs fell from 19.5 million in 1979 to under 11.5 million during the pandemic period referenced in the data [Source: ev-1]. Conversely, finance and professional services grew from 12 million to 32 million jobs, concentrating high-income professionals in urban cores [Source: ev-1]. In San Francisco specifically, top incomes rose by approximately $120,000 between 2014 and 2016 [Source: ev-1]. Federal Reserve data tracking over 3,140 inequality series confirms that inequality reached record levels by 2018 through 2021, with the U.S. showing the sharpest increase among advanced economies since the 1980 [Source: ev-1].
